newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Australia markets look to US data.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Australia markets look to US data.

text.p: Australian markets will focus on a wealth of statistics due out this week, following losses on Wall Street late last week which trimmed Tuesday's strong rise.

Wall Street fell about 20 points on Thursday and another 53 points on Friday as investors set themselves for a series of economic reports seen as settling questions about the outlook for interest rates.

Figures due for release include the first quarter employment cost index on Tuesday, first quarter GDP on Wednesday, the April purchasing manager's report on Thursday and April non-farm payrolls on Friday.

"This data is likely to confirm a U.S. economy still motoring along well above its long-term trend line, with all the associated potential negatives for the medium term inflation outlook," Westpac Banking Corp said in a market commentary.
Westpac said it expected the U.S. Federal Reserve to lift U.S. rates by 25 basis points to 5.75 percent after the FOMC meeting on May 20.
Domestic data includes the March balance on goods and trades and services, average weekly earnings for the February quarter, and building approvals and retail trade figures for March.
ECONOMIC DATA

Data is scarce during the early part of the week, as market attention is expected to increasingly focus on next month's budget, with Wednesday's March balance on goods and services the first major local figure.
The trade balance is expected to remain in surplus, but be down on February's surprisingly large A$336 million surplus.
Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) deputy governor Stephen Grenville will speak on Monday at a conference in Sydney on forecasting the Australian economy.
RBA insights may prove valuable as the question of another rate cut has come back into play over recent weeks following weak employment data and continuing good news on the inflation and wages front.

The next update on wages is due on Thursday, when average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) for the March quarter are due. The release is expected to be paradoxical for markets, as it is forecast to contain the lowest quarterly increase for one year, but also the highest annual rate since the first quarter of last year.
An AWOTE figure above four percent may be a concern for markets, but the fact that private sector AWOTE is running at just three percent is expected to limit negative reaction.

Thursday also sees the release of March building approvals data, and the market will be seeing if the early signs of a 1997 recovery led by housing are on target, or if expectations should be revised down.
One figure that is expected to put a dent in the case of the case for a rate cut is Friday's retail trade data. After two strong months in Janaury and February, a flat result is expected in March.

However, the strong start to the quarter means that a strong rise in real terms is widely forecast, and given the first quarter strength seen in motor vehicle registrations, private consumption is expected to be a strong contributor to first quarter economic growth.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS: Thu, 10-year bond yield 7.87 pct +0.04

The Australian bond market faces a steady flow of data on two fronts next week with local indicators possibly suggesting that the Reserve Bank will ease policy again and key U.S. reports confirming that the Federal Reserve will tighten in May.
Retail trade and building approvals data may add some spice to speculation that the RBA will ease after benign inflation and wages outcome last week if they prove weak.
But the market will also be apprehensive about average weekly earnings data and will want to make sure this remains within the RBA's 4.0-4.5 percent comfort zone.
A small community of local analysts see the opportunity for the RBA to ease again, given the patchy recovery and unemployment stuck at high levels.
This week's releases could swell their numbers.
However, the U.S. data due out could prove the key focus for the market, with first quarter GDP, the NAPM index and non-farm payrolls all seen as major releases.
AUSTRALIAN FOREX: Thu, US$0.7756/61 Wed,US$0.7777/82
The Australian dollar will be led by a raft of domestic and international economic data due out this week after spending last week bouncing around in a broad US$0.7690/7795 band.

A break of US$0.7680 or US$0.7820 would end the deadlock and, given the large stops that were believed to be building either side, could easily see a 1/2 cent lunge afterwards with US$0.7630 and US$0.7895 the big technical targets.

The currency ended last week quietly ahead of Friday's national ANZAC Day holiday in Australia. The unit took a defensive stance at US$0.7756/61 after slipping from US$0.7777/82 late Wednesday, but was up on a US$0.7735 low.
Figures of importance this week will be Q1 average weekly earnings and March building approvals Thursday, and retail trade for March and the first quarter on Friday.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS: Thu, All Ords Index 2,474.70 +2.40
Australian equities are likely to start the week nervously after falls on Wall Street on Thursday and Friday while the local market was out of action for Anzac Day.
Wall Street gave up 20 points on Thursday and another 53 on Friday following Tuesday's 173 point gain. The losses capped the rally for the week to about 35 points.
Local fundamentals will remain prominent following the resilient tone seen in recent weeks, although strong performances from Wall Street would undoubtedly help proceedings.

"I think there is room for a little bit more upside. Even on the down days, no-one seem to want to hit anything too hard. I think people are happy enough with the way its going," said Phillip Toop of Lance Jones.

Underlining the solid local fundamentals, the benchmark All Ordinaries index has gained more than 120 points since its 70 point slump on April 1, rising from that day's close of 2,352.2 to 2,474.7 last Thursday.
U.S. short term gyrations were not seen as critical, although a confirmed bearish trend would put a brake on local buying interest.
"We will probably still need a bit of positive sentiment to flow through from overseas. Even if we don't strictly follow them, we need that sentiment to keep things going," Toop said.
Corporate news is thin on the ground, although base metals miner North Ltd will deliver its third quarter results on Monday and chemical group ICI Australia its half year results on Wednesday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
